- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 2–5% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.
- If model forecast is rising sharply after a recent spike (e.g., +0.5–1.0% per day), reduce forecast by 1–3% to avoid overshoot and lagged correction.
- If official event net supply is negative and sentiment is bearish (≤0.33), model should not overcorrect downward — allow 1–2% buffer below recent low to avoid mean reversion trap.
- When sentiment swings from bullish to bearish within 3–5 days, model should not lag more than 2 days — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment shift within 1–2 days.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >10% from 14-day moving average, apply mean reversion correction: forecast = 14-day MA ± 1.5×σ (if volatility >0.5%).
- If recent auction supply events are frequent (≥3/30d) and sentiment is neutral or bearish, reduce forecast slope by 0.1–0.3% per day to reflect supply pressure.
- If model forecast is below 65% of 14-day MA and sentiment is bullish, increase forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
- For high event count (≥20/30d) with net supply negative, model should not overpredict decline — cap downward slope at -0.2% per day unless sentiment confirms bearish.
- If sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33) and model is flat, forecast should be adjusted downward by 0.5–1.5% per day to reflect bearish sentiment bias.
- If model forecast is above 75% of 14-day MA and sentiment is bearish, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day to avoid overcorrection.
